mechanisms-intro-s1.title: A proposed mechanism for making water from NO and H₂
mechanisms-intro-s1.html:
The overall reaction 2 NO(g) + 2 H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2 H₂O(g) is proposed to happen in three elementary steps:

  1. 2 NO → N₂O₂
  2. N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O
  3. N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O

mechanisms-intro-s2.title: Two mechanisms proposed for one reaction
mechanisms-intro-s2.html:
The overall reaction is 2 O₃(g) → 3 O₂(g). Two students propose mechanisms. In each, every step occurs once each time the overall reaction occurs.

Mechanism X

  1. O₃ → O₂ + O
  2. O + O₃ → 2 O₂

Mechanism Y

  1. O₃ → O₂ + O
  2. O + O → O₂

mechanism-rate-laws-s1.title: Rate data and two proposed mechanisms
mechanism-rate-laws-s1.html:
For NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) at a fixed temperature, a student measures initial rates:

Mechanism 1 (one step): NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂

Mechanism 2: step 1 (slow): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂

mechanism-rate-laws-s2.title: A two-step mechanism for making NOBr
mechanism-rate-laws-s2.html:
One proposed mechanism for 2 NO(g) + Br₂(g) → 2 NOBr(g):

  1. NO + Br₂ → NOBr₂ (slow)
  2. NOBr₂ + NO → 2 NOBr (fast)

pre-equilibrium-s1.title: A fast reversible first step
pre-equilibrium-s1.html:
A proposed mechanism for 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g):

  1. NO + NO ⇌ N₂O₂  (fast, reversible; k₁ = 2.0 × 10³ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ forward, k₋₁ = 5.0 × 10⁴ s⁻¹ back)
  2. N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂  (slow; k₂ = 1.5 × 10² M⁻¹ s⁻¹)

pre-equilibrium-s2.title: Testing mechanisms for hydrogen iodide
pre-equilibrium-s2.html:
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2 HI(g) at a fixed high temperature, initial rates were measured:

Mechanism P: H₂ + I₂ → 2 HI (one step).

Mechanism Q: (1) I₂ ⇌ 2 I (fast, reversible); (2) H₂ + 2 I → 2 HI (slow).

Initial concentrations and initial rates

catalysis-s1.title: Hydrogen peroxide with iodide ions
catalysis-s1.html:
Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly on its own: 2 H₂O₂(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Adding a little potassium iodide makes it fizz quickly. A proposed mechanism:

  1. H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻ (slow)
  2. H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻ (fast)

items.q: Which species are intermediates in this mechanism? Select all that apply.
options: N₂O₂
N₂O
H₂
H₂O

items.q: Does the mechanism add up to the overall reaction?
options: Yes: the intermediates cancel and the sum matches
No: the steps make just one H₂O in total
No: N₂O₂ is left over at the end
Yes, provided step 1 is written twice

items.q: What is the molecularity of step 2?
options: Unimolecular
Bimolecular
Termolecular
Tetramolecular

items.q: Why is the overall reaction proposed to go by these steps rather than in one step?
options: One step would need four molecules to collide at once
One step would make different products
One step would have no activation energy
One step would use up the intermediates

items.q: In the lab, a chemist detects N₂O in the reaction flask partway through, but not at the end. How does this relate to the mechanism?
options: It supports the mechanism: N₂O is an intermediate made and then used
It disproves the mechanism: N₂O is not in the overall equation
It shows N₂O is a product that later escapes the flask
It shows N₂O is a reactant that was left over

items.q: Which mechanism adds up to the overall reaction?
options: Mechanism X
Mechanism Y
Both mechanisms
Neither mechanism

items.q: In mechanism X, what is the oxygen atom, O?
options: An intermediate
A reactant
A product
A transition state

items.q: Mechanism Y also needs two O atoms to meet. Why is that step unlikely to be important in this reaction?
options: O atoms are scarce, so two rarely meet
O atoms do not form a bond with each other
Two O atoms would make O₃, not O₂
The step is termolecular, which is rare

items.q: A third student proposes the one-step mechanism 2 O₃ → 3 O₂. Which statement is true?
options: It sums correctly; data are needed to decide
It is wrong, since a mechanism has two or more steps
It is right, since it matches the overall equation exactly
It is wrong, since it has no intermediate

items.q: A mechanism has the steps: (1) Br₂ → 2 Br; (2) Br + H₂ → HBr + H; (3) H + Br₂ → HBr + Br. Which species are intermediates? Select all that apply.
options: Br
H
H₂
HBr

items.q: The mechanism (1) A + B → C; (2) C + B → D is proposed. What is the overall reaction?
options: A + 2 B → D
A + B → D
A + B + C → C + D
C + B → D

items.q: Which statement about a reaction mechanism is correct?
options: A series of elementary steps that sums to the overall reaction
The balanced overall equation, written out with state symbols
The list of the products, in the order in which they form
The rate law of the reaction, as measured in the lab

items.q: A proposed mechanism for 2 NO₂Cl → 2 NO₂ + Cl₂ is: (1) NO₂Cl → NO₂ + Cl; (2) ? Each step occurs once each time the overall reaction occurs. Which second step completes it?
options: NO₂Cl + Cl → NO₂ + Cl₂
Cl + Cl → Cl₂
NO₂ + Cl → NO₂Cl
NO₂Cl → NO₂ + Cl

items.q: Why are intermediates hard to collect from a reaction mixture?
options: They react in a later step soon after they form
They are the same as the transition states
They form after the reaction is over
They are present in larger amounts than the products

items.q: A student says, "N₂O₂ appears in the mechanism, so it should appear in the overall equation too." Which response is best?
options: N₂O₂ is made and then used, so it cancels from the sum
The student is right; the overall equation is missing N₂O₂
N₂O₂ is a transition state, which is left out of equations
N₂O₂ is left out because it is a gas

items.q: What is the experimental rate law?
options: rate = k[NO₂]²
rate = k[NO₂][CO]
rate = k[NO₂]
rate = k[NO₂]²[CO]

items.q: Which mechanism is consistent with the data, and why?
options: Mechanism 2: its slow step gives k[NO₂]²
Mechanism 1: it is the same as the overall equation
Mechanism 1: a one-step path is simpler than two
Both: they each add up to the overall equation

items.q: In mechanism 2, why does [CO] not appear in the rate law?
options: CO reacts in the fast step, after the slow one
CO is an intermediate that cancels out
CO is a product of the slow step
CO is present in a large excess in the trials

items.q: From trial 2 and the rate law consistent with mechanism 2, what is the value of k for the NO₂ + CO reaction? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: square [NO₂]. The rate law is second order in NO₂: k = rate/[NO₂]².
Value: CO is zero order, so leave [CO] out when you solve for k.

items.q: What rate law does this mechanism predict?
options: rate = k[NO][Br₂]
rate = k[NO]²[Br₂]
rate = k[NOBr₂][NO]
rate = k[NO]²

items.q: Which species is the intermediate in this mechanism?
options: NOBr₂
NO
Br₂
NOBr

items.q: Experiments show rate = k[NO]²[Br₂]. What does this tell you about the mechanism above?
options: It is not consistent with the data
It is consistent, since it sums to the overall equation
It is consistent, since it has a slow step
The data are wrong, since they match the overall coefficients

items.q: Suppose this mechanism is correct. Predict how each change affects the overall rate.

variables.name: Overall rate if step 2 were made ten times faster

items.q: What is the rate-determining step of a mechanism?
options: The slowest step, which limits the overall rate
The first step of a mechanism, whatever its speed
The step with the greatest number of reactant molecules
The step in which the final product is made

items.q: A mechanism is: (1) 2 A → A₂ (slow); (2) A₂ + B → A₂B (fast). What is the predicted rate law?
options: rate = k[A]²
rate = k[A]²[B]
rate = k[A₂][B]
rate = k[A][B]

items.q: The overall reaction X + 2 Y → Z has the measured rate law rate = k[X]. Which statement about its mechanism is most reasonable?
options: A slow first step uses X alone; Y reacts in later fast steps
The mechanism is one step in which X and two Y collide
Y is an intermediate, so it is left out of the rate law
The slowest step uses two Y and no X

items.q: In a mechanism, step 1 is slow and step 2 is fast. A chemist finds a way to make step 2 twice as fast. What happens to the overall rate?
options: It halves
It stays about the same
It doubles
It becomes four times as fast

items.q: Two mechanisms both sum to the overall equation and both predict the measured rate law. What can you conclude?
options: Both are consistent with the data; more evidence is needed
The one with fewer steps is the correct mechanism
Both are proven correct at the same time
Neither can be correct, since mechanisms are unique

items.q: Measured: rate = k[H₂][ICl] for H₂ + 2 ICl → I₂ + 2 HCl. Which mechanism is consistent?
options: (1) H₂ + ICl → HI + HCl, slow; (2) HI + ICl → I₂ + HCl, fast
(1) H₂ + ICl → HI + HCl, fast; (2) HI + ICl → I₂ + HCl, slow
One step: H₂ + 2 ICl → I₂ + 2 HCl
(1) 2 ICl → I₂ + Cl₂, slow; (2) H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, fast

items.q: A mechanism's slow first step is A + B → C, with k = 3.2 × 10⁻² M⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the predicted overall rate, in M/s, when [A] = 0.25 M and [B] = 0.40 M?

mistakes.why: Value: the slow step is bimolecular, so include [B]: rate = k[A][B].
Value: A has coefficient 1 in the slow step, so it is first order; do not square [A].

items.q: What is the rate law of the slow step, written as it stands?
options: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂]
rate = k₂[NO]²[O₂]
rate = k₂[NO₂]²
rate = k₂[NO][O₂]

items.q: Setting the forward and back rates of step 1 equal, what is [N₂O₂]?
options: (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]²
(k₋₁/k₁)[NO]²
(k₁/k₋₁)[NO]
k₁k₋₁[NO]²

items.q: What overall rate law does the mechanism predict?
options: rate = k[NO]²[O₂]
rate = k[NO][O₂]
rate = k[N₂O₂][O₂]
rate = k[NO]²

items.q: Using the constants given, calculate the overall rate constant k = k₂k₁/k₋₁. Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is inverted. [N₂O₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]², so k = k₂k₁/k₋₁.
Value: k₋₁ goes in the denominator, not the numerator.

items.q: What is the experimental rate law?
options: rate = k[H₂][I₂]
rate = k[H₂]²[I₂]
rate = k[H₂][I₂]²
rate = k[I₂]

items.q: What rate law does mechanism Q predict?
options: rate = k[H₂][I₂]
rate = k[H₂][I]²
rate = k[H₂][I₂]²
rate = k[I₂]

items.q: Which conclusion is justified by the data?
options: Both fit; rate data do not separate them
Q fits and P does not, because Q has a reversible step
P fits and Q does not, because P is a single step
Neither fits, because I atoms are missing from the rate law

items.q: In mechanism Q, why can the first step be treated as having equal forward and back rates?
options: It runs fast both ways compared with step 2
I atoms do not react with H₂ here
The slow step uses up the I₂ as soon as it forms
The first step has no activation energy

items.q: Why must a rate law be written without the concentration of an intermediate?
options: Its concentration is not set by the experimenter
An intermediate has a concentration of exactly zero throughout
Intermediates are transition states
Intermediates exist just in solids

items.q: Mechanism: (1) NO + Br₂ ⇌ NOBr₂ (fast, reversible); (2) NOBr₂ + NO → 2 NOBr (slow). What rate law does it predict?
options: rate = k[NO]²[Br₂]
rate = k[NO][Br₂]
rate = k[NOBr₂][NO]
rate = k[NO]²

items.q: For the mechanism NO + Br₂ ⇌ NOBr₂ (fast), NOBr₂ + NO → 2 NOBr (slow), predict each change in the initial rate.

variables.name: Rate when NOBr (product) is added at the start

items.q: In a proposed pathway, X and Y quickly form XY and XY quickly falls apart again; then XY reacts slowly with a second Y to give the product. Which rate law follows?
options: rate = k[X][Y]²
rate = k[X][Y]
rate = k[XY][Y]
rate = k[X]²[Y]

items.q: In the fast reversible step NO + NO ⇌ N₂O₂, k₁ = 2.0 × 10³ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ and k₋₁ = 5.0 × 10⁴ s⁻¹. What is [N₂O₂], in M, when [NO] = 0.010 M?

mistakes.why: Value: two NO molecules react in step 1, so square [NO].
Value: the ratio is inverted. From k₁[NO]² = k₋₁[N₂O₂], [N₂O₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]².

items.q: A student writes the rate law for a mechanism with a fast reversible first step as rate = k₂[H₂][I]² and stops. What is missing?
options: Replacing [I] using the balanced fast step
Adding the coefficients of the overall equation as exponents
Multiplying by the forward rate constant of the fast step
Nothing; intermediates belong in rate laws

items.q: In a mechanism with a fast reversible first step and a slow second step, which step is rate-determining?
options: The fast first step, since it comes first
The slow second step
Both steps equally
Neither; a reversible step has no rate

items.q: Where is the intermediate C on the profile?
options: In the valley between the two peaks, at 80 kJ/mol
At the first peak, at 140 kJ/mol
At the second peak, at 110 kJ/mol
At the right-hand plateau, at 20 kJ/mol

items.q: What is the activation energy of step 2, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: you measured from the reactants (50). Step 2 starts at the intermediate (80 kJ/mol): 110 − 80.
Value: that is the energy of the second transition state. Subtract the level step 2 starts from.

items.q: Which step is rate-determining, and what is the evidence?
options: Step 1: its barrier, 90 kJ/mol, is larger
Step 2: its transition state comes later in the reaction
Step 2: its barrier ends nearest to the products
Step 1: being first, it is the slowest by rule

items.q: What rate law does this profile predict for the overall reaction A + B → D?
options: rate = k[A][B]
rate = k[C]
rate = k[A][B][C]
rate = k[D]

items.q: What is the overall energy change for A + B → D, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the products (20) are below the reactants (50), so energy is released and the change is negative.
Value: compare the products with the reactants, not with the intermediate: 20 − 50.

items.q: What is the activation energy of step 2, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: step 2 starts from intermediate 1 (20 kJ/mol), not from the reactants.
Value: that runs from transition state 2 down to intermediate 2. Step 2 climbs from intermediate 1 up to transition state 2.

items.q: Which step is rate-determining?
options: Step 1 (Ea = 45 kJ/mol)
Step 2 (Ea = 75 kJ/mol)
Step 3 (Ea = 50 kJ/mol)
Step 3, since it releases the most energy

items.q: How many intermediates does this mechanism have, and how many transition states?
options: 2 intermediates and 2 transition states
2 intermediates and 3 transition states
3 intermediates and 2 transition states
3 intermediates and 3 transition states

items.q: What is the overall energy change of the reaction, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the products are below the reactants, so the change is negative.
Value: you compared the products with intermediate 2 (−60 − (−10)). The overall change is products minus reactants: −60 − 0.

items.q: On a multistep energy profile, what does each peak represent?
options: The transition state of one elementary step
An intermediate that can be isolated
The products of the overall reaction
A point where no bonds are changing

items.q: A two-step profile shows a deep valley below the reactant level (a very stable intermediate) and a second peak higher than the first. A student says, "Step 1 is first, so it must be the slow step." Which response is best?
options: Step 2 has the larger climb from its valley, so it is slower
The student is right; the first step is the slow one
Both steps are equally slow, since there are two peaks
The deep valley means the reaction does not happen

items.q: For a two-step reaction, step 1 has Ea = 60 kJ/mol and step 2 has Ea = 25 kJ/mol. The reactants are at 0 kJ/mol and the intermediate at 35 kJ/mol. What is the energy of the second transition state?
options: 25 kJ/mol
35 kJ/mol
60 kJ/mol
85 kJ/mol

items.q: A two-step reaction has a slow first step. Suppose step 2 were changed so its barrier became even smaller, with nothing else changed. Predict each effect.
A three-step reaction profile is drawn. How many valleys lie between the reactant and product plateaus?
Why is an intermediate on an energy profile drawn in a valley rather than at a peak?
options: It is a real, if short-lived, species that sits at a local minimum
It has more energy than both transition states around it
It forms after the reaction is complete
It is the same as the transition state

items.q: In this mechanism, what is the role of I⁻?
options: A catalyst: used in step 1 and remade in step 2
An intermediate: made in step 1 and used in step 2
A reactant: used up as the reaction goes
A product: made in step 2

items.q: Which species is an intermediate?
options: IO⁻
I⁻
H₂O₂
O₂

items.q: What rate law does the mechanism predict?
options: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]
rate = k[H₂O₂]²
rate = k[H₂O₂][IO⁻]
rate = k[H₂O₂]

items.q: A student doubles the amount of KI added (same H₂O₂). Predict each change.

variables.name: Total volume of O₂ collected at the end
Amount of I⁻ in solution at the end
Overall energy change of the reaction

items.q: A student says, "I⁻ is in the rate law, so it must be a reactant that is used up." Which evidence refutes this?
options: The two steps sum to an equation without I⁻; it is remade
IO⁻ does not appear in the rate law
The reaction fizzes more when KI is added
The rate law is first order in H₂O₂

items.q: By how much, in kJ/mol, does the catalyst lower the highest point that the reacting particles must pass?

mistakes.why: Value: compare the highest peak on each path: 185 (uncatalyzed) and 135 (catalyzed, second peak), not the first catalyzed peak.
Value: the overall energy change (25 − 60) is the same for both paths; compare the peaks instead.

items.q: Which statement about the two pathways is supported by the graph?
options: Both release 35 kJ/mol; the catalyzed path has two steps
The catalyzed path releases more energy than the uncatalyzed one
The catalyst raises the energy of the products
Both pathways have one step and one transition state

items.q: Why is the catalyzed reaction faster at the same temperature?
options: Its highest barrier is lower, so more collisions succeed
The catalyst gives the molecules extra kinetic energy
The catalyst makes the products more stable
The catalyzed path has more steps, and more steps are faster

items.q: What is the activation energy of the first step of the catalyzed path, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the peak's energy. Subtract the starting level (60 kJ/mol).
Value: that is the second step (135 − 95). The first step climbs from the reactants at 60 to the first peak at 125.

items.q: Which statements about a catalyst are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It is regenerated by the end of the reaction
It changes the energy difference between reactants and products
It raises the kinetic energy of the reacting molecules
It is a reactant that appears in the overall equation

items.q: In the mechanism (1) A + Q → AQ; (2) AQ + B → AB + Q, which is the catalyst and which is the intermediate?
options: Catalyst Q; intermediate AQ
Catalyst AQ; intermediate Q
Catalyst B; intermediate AB
Catalyst A; intermediate Q

items.q: In a car's catalytic converter, harmful gases react on the surface of solid platinum. Which statement explains how the metal speeds the reaction?
options: Gas molecules stick to the metal, which weakens their bonds and lowers the barrier
The metal reacts with the gases and is gradually used up
The hot metal gives each molecule enough energy to react
The metal absorbs the products so the reaction can go further

items.q: A student claims, "A catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction, so it makes more product." Which response is best?
options: It lowers the barrier both ways; the product amount is unchanged
Correct: a catalyst speeds up the forward reaction and gives a higher yield
A catalyst slows the reverse reaction, which is why more product forms
A catalyst speeds up just the reverse reaction

items.q: A reaction's activation energy is 132 kJ/mol without a catalyst and 87 kJ/mol with one. By what percentage does the catalyst lower the activation energy?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the drop by the original barrier (132), not by the new one.
Value: that is the new barrier as a percentage of the old one. Subtract it from 100% to get the decrease.

items.q: Enzymes are protein catalysts. Why does a small amount of enzyme speed up the reaction of a large amount of reactant?
options: Each enzyme molecule is regenerated and reused many times
Each enzyme molecule reacts with the whole sample at once
The enzyme is used up, but it releases energy as it reacts
The enzyme raises the temperature of the mixture

items.q: Which observation would show that a substance added to a reaction is a catalyst rather than a reactant?
options: Its amount is the same at the end as at the start
The reaction mixture changes color when it is added
It appears in the measured rate law
The reaction gives off more heat when it is added
